questions.prompt: A nullable PostgreSQL column has an ordinary UNIQUE constraint. Two rows both contain NULL in that column. What does the default null treatment allow?

choices.text: The second NULL is rejected.
Both rows can exist.
The first NULL is automatically replaced with a generated non-null value.
Both rows are deleted when the constraint is validated at transaction end.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL treats nulls as distinct for uniqueness by default. NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that behavior; ordinary uniqueness does not substitute or delete values.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.5. Constraints
sources.claim: PostgreSQL unique constraints treat nulls as distinct by default; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes null equality for uniqueness.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL transaction temporarily violates a DEFERRABLE foreign key set to DEFERRED, then repairs it before commit. When is that deferred check required?

choices.text: Before every modified row.
Only after the next VACUUM has scanned the referenced table.
At transaction end.
Never, because DEFERRABLE permanently disables the foreign key.

questions.explanation: Deferral postpones constraint checking to transaction end, allowing a temporary violation that is repaired before commit. It does not remove the constraint.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: CREATE TABLE
sources.claim: DEFERRABLE constraints can be checked at transaction end; CHECK and NOT NULL constraints cannot be deferred.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table uses CHECK (price > 0) on a nullable price column. Which properties matter? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The CHECK alone rejects every NULL price automatically.
The CHECK is re-evaluated on every other row whenever any price changes.
A NULL price satisfies this CHECK constraint.
NOT NULL is needed separately if missing prices must be rejected.
Cross-row consistency should use a suitable relational constraint instead of CHECK.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: a null result satisfies CHECK. B is incorrect: CHECK constraints concern the inserted or updated row, not a cross-row invariant scan. C is correct: a CHECK passes when its result is true or null. D is correct: the comparison CHECK does not reject a null result. E is correct: CHECK is not supported as a reliable constraint over other rows.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.5. Constraints
sources.claim: A CHECK constraint is satisfied by true or null and does not enforce NOT NULL; PostgreSQL does not support CHECK constraints relying on other rows for consistency.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL 15+ design needs a nullable unique key to permit at most one NULL. Which constraint option directly changes the null comparison?

choices.text: UNIQUE DEFERRABLE.
UNIQUE USING INDEX, which always prohibits any null entry.
UNIQUE NOT VALID, which treats every missing value as the same key.
UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT

questions.explanation: NULLS NOT DISTINCT makes nulls compare equal for the uniqueness check. Deferring a check changes its timing rather than its null equality.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.5. Constraints
sources.claim: PostgreSQL unique constraints treat nulls as distinct by default; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes null equality for uniqueness.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL team wants to defer a CHECK constraint until commit by declaring it DEFERRABLE. Which limitation applies?

choices.text: CHECK constraints cannot be deferred.
Every CHECK is already deferred.
Deferral is supported only when the CHECK refers to another table.
The CHECK becomes deferrable automatically if its expression returns NULL.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports deferral for eligible uniqueness, primary key, exclusion and foreign key constraints. CHECK and NOT NULL constraints are not deferrable.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: CREATE TABLE
sources.claim: DEFERRABLE constraints can be checked at transaction end; CHECK and NOT NULL constraints cannot be deferred.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL designer treats CHECK constraints as persistent assertions. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A false CHECK expression rejects the candidate row.
PostgreSQL assumes the CHECK condition is immutable for a given row.
A CHECK function may change behavior later without any need to revalidate old rows.
CHECK guarantees a cross-table count stays below a threshold after every commit.
CHECK (value > 0) is equivalent to value NOT NULL plus the positivity rule.

questions.explanation: A is correct: false violates the check constraint. B is correct: it does not continuously reevaluate unchanged rows when external function behavior changes. C is incorrect: changing such behavior can leave old rows violating the intended condition. D is incorrect: checks over other rows or tables do not provide that supported guarantee. E is incorrect: the CHECK accepts null whereas NOT NULL rejects it.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.5. Constraints
sources.claim: A CHECK constraint is satisfied by true or null and does not enforce NOT NULL; PostgreSQL does not support CHECK constraints relying on other rows for consistency.
